title: What is Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) — it pushes 0..N elements to a Consumer instead of returning a sub-stream like flatMap — when is it more efficient, and how do you use it?
shortTitle: Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) — push 0..N elements imperatively, vs flatMap

s1_definition.profdef: `mapMulti(BiConsumer<T, Consumer<R>>)` (Java 16) is an intermediate operation where you PUSH elements to a downstream Consumer instead of creating a Stream (like flatMap). For each input element, you call `consumer.accept(output)` zero, one, or many times. More efficient than flatMap when: (1) producing 0 or 1 elements per input (no Stream.of/Stream.empty overhead), (2) imperative logic is needed (loops, conditions), (3) avoiding per-element Stream object allocation.
s1_definition.analogy: flatMap: each clerk creates a TRAY of items and puts the tray on the belt. mapMulti: each clerk directly PLACES items on the belt one by one — no tray needed. For one or zero items per clerk, skipping the tray saves time.
s1_definition.oneliner: mapMulti((element, consumer) → { consumer.accept(output); }) = push elements imperatively. Fewer intermediate Stream objects than flatMap. Java 16+.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `mapMulti(BiConsumer<T, Consumer<R>>)` (Java 16) is an intermediate operation where you PUSH elements to a downstream Consumer instead of creating a Stream (like flatMap). For each input element, you call `consumer.accept(output)` zero, one, or many times. More efficient than flatMap when: (1) producing 0 or 1 elements per input (no Stream.of/Stream.empty overhead), (2) imperative logic is needed (loops, conditions), (3) avoiding per-element Stream object allocation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** flatMap: each clerk creates a TRAY of items and puts the tray on the belt. mapMulti: each clerk directly PLACES items on the belt one by one — no tray needed. For one or zero items per clerk, skipping the tray saves time.

**One line to remember:** mapMulti((element, consumer) → { consumer.accept(output); }) = push elements imperatively. Fewer intermediate Stream objects than flatMap. Java 16+.

sections.s2_technical:
`Stream.mapMulti` (Java 16) is an imperative alternative to `flatMap` for one-to-many mapping. Instead of returning a new stream per element, you receive a `Consumer` ("downstream") and PUSH zero or more output elements into it: `stream.mapMulti((trade, downstream) -> { if (trade.isSplit()) { downstream.accept(leg1); downstream.accept(leg2); } else downstream.accept(trade); })`.

The advantage over `flatMap` is efficiency when each element usually produces zero or one result, or a small known number: `flatMap` allocates a `Stream` object per element even to emit one value, whereas `mapMulti` just calls `downstream.accept` with no intermediate stream allocation. This matters in hot paths over large datasets.

A banking example: expanding block trades into their constituent legs — most trades emit themselves (one accept), but a block trade emits several legs — done with `mapMulti` to avoid creating a throwaway stream for the common single-leg case. Senior nuance: prefer `flatMap` for readability when each element naturally maps to a collection/stream; reach for `mapMulti` as a performance optimisation when the per-element stream allocation of `flatMap` is measurable, or when the emission logic is naturally imperative.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Expanding block trades into legs with `flatMap` allocated a throwaway stream for every trade, even the common case of a single-leg trade, hurting a hot settlement path. Fix: `mapMulti` pushes output legs into a downstream consumer with no per-element stream allocation, so single-leg trades cost nothing extra and block trades emit multiple legs.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: trades T1 (1 leg) and T2 (3 legs).

**Step 2.** `mapMulti((t, downstream) -> ...)` receives each trade and a downstream Consumer to push outputs into.

**Step 3.** For T1 it pushes one leg T1-L1 (no stream allocated); for T2 it pushes three legs T2-L1, T2-L2, T2-L3.

**Step 4.** The pushed elements form the single output stream directly.

**Step 5.** The expanded legs [T1-L1, T2-L1, T2-L2, T2-L3] are produced without per-element stream objects.

```text
INFO: expanded=[T1-L1, T2-L1, T2-L2, T2-L3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  trades: T1(1 leg), T2(3 legs)
    │ mapMulti((t, downstream) -> push legs)
    ├─ T1 → downstream.accept("T1-L1")                 (no stream allocated)
    └─ T2 → accept L1, accept L2, accept L3
    ▼
  [T1-L1, T2-L1, T2-L2, T2-L3]
  vs flatMap: allocates a Stream per element (even for 1 leg)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) pushes elements to a Consumer imperatively instead of returning a Stream like flatMap. More efficient for: 0-or-1 element production (avoids Stream.of/Stream.empty allocation per element), imperative logic (loops, conditions), and primitive variants (mapMultiToInt avoids boxing). Use flatMap when the mapping naturally produces a Stream (Collection::stream). Use mapMulti when the mapping is conditional (filter+transform) or involves imperative loops.
